segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I'm writing my birthday wish list, Beth. Listen, I want a new laptop, a gold Rolex watch and a red sports car.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Phew, that is quite a lot, Neil. Isn't that a bit greedy?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So what? Greed is good. We're genetically built to want things that increase our social status, power and material possessions like money, a nice house, a fast car, all that stuff.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm not so sure, Neil. Remember, greed is also one of the seven deadly sins.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In this programme, we'll be discussing greed, the desire to accumulate stuff, keep it for yourself and not share it with others.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And of course, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary as well.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: You reminded me of a famous quote by one of history's greatest leaders.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The world has enough for everyone's need, but not everyone's greed.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But who said it?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Was it A, the Dalai Lama, B, Mahatma Gandhi, or C, Martin Luther King?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I think it was Mahatma Gandhi.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK Beth, I'll reveal the correct answer at the end of the programme.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: At the neurological level greed is controlled by the reward centre of the brain Greedy people feel good when they choose the stuff they want and this happens at the unconscious emotional level of the brain meaning there little

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: conscious awareness about how greedy actions might affect others or be unfair.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But what does this look like in real life? That's what University of California psychologist

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Professor Paul Pith investigated using the classic family board game Monopoly. The game

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: was rigged to give one rich player an advantage by letting them roll two dice instead of one,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and collecting twice as much money as the poor player when passing go.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So what happened when Professor Piff asked the rich players why they had inevitably won the fixed

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: game? Listen to the answer he gave to BBC Radio 4 programme Seven Deadly Psychologies.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: They took credit for their wins. They talked about how they'd controlled their own outcomes.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: They talked about how it was the decisions they'd made that had led to their being ultimately

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: victorious and not that flip of a coin that randomly got them into that position of privilege

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: in the first place. Now, I don't know that this is a perfect model for how privilege,

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: success or wealth operates in everyday life.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: Some people indeed have worked themselves up

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: by their own bootstraps and get what they have

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: because they worked hard.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Interestingly the rich players took credit for winning If you take credit for something you accept praise and recognition for doing something whether or not that praise and recognition is deserved

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In fact, it was the fixed game that determined who would win and lose, not anything the players did.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Professor Piff uses the expression the flip of a coin to describe something which is based solely on random chance,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: like when you flip a coin into the air.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Whether it lands on heads or tails is pure luck.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yet the winning players claimed they won thanks to their own skill and ability.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here, Professor Piff uses another idiom to pull yourself up by your bootstraps,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: meaning to improve your situation through your own hard work, without help from anyone else.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Worryingly, the experiment showed how feeling financially better off than others

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: can easily change into feeling better than others.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And the reason behind these feelings could be what money buys you, especially one thing, space.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you're rich, you own a big house. At work, you have your own spacious private office.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: You live in your own private bubble.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Professor Piff again, talking with BBC Radio 4's Seven Deadly Psychologies.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: People who are well off are just more socially independent.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: They don't need others in their lives as much.

segments.speaker: Professor Paul Piff
segments.text: And when you don't need others, well, your empathy might suffer as a result.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: People who are well and rich enough to do what they want rely on other people less As a result they may lack empathy the ability to share someone else feelings

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: by imagining what it would be like to be them.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Maybe it's not greed itself that's bad, but the things we're greedy for.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Being greedy for social justice or a clean environment is good, right?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Something to be admired by the world leader in your question, Neil.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Yes, I asked you who said the world has enough for everyone's need but not everyone's greed.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: You said it was Mahatma Gandhi, which was the correct answer, Beth.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned from this programme, starting with stuff, an informal word for material possessions.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: To take credit for something means to allow people to believe that something you did deserves praise or recognition.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The phrase a flip of a coin refers to an action or decision based on luck or random chance.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you pull yourself up by your bootstraps, you improve your situation through your own efforts, without help from anyone else.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Someone who is well off is rich enough to be able to have most of what they want.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And finally, empathy means experiencing someone else's feelings by putting yourself in their place.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up. Join us again soon for more trending topics and useful vocabulary here at 6 Minute English. Goodbye for now!

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Goodbye!
